definition.text: An upgrade of the 20th-century electrical grid that uses two-way communications and distributed intelligent devices.

facts.text: Classic grids were centralized, one-way systems of transmission, distribution and demand-driven control; two-way flows of electricity and information could improve delivery.
Smart grids use techniques such as state estimation to detect faults and self-heal without technician intervention, improving reliability and reducing vulnerability to disasters or attacks.
They handle bidirectional flows from rooftop solar and electric-car batteries; classic grids assumed one-way flow, so local over-generation can raise safety issues.
Smart grid flexibility allows more variable renewables such as solar and wind, even without added storage.
Demand response lets generators and loads coordinate in real time to flatten spikes, avoiding reserve generators and letting users run low-priority devices when energy is cheapest.
Smart grids let suppliers and consumers exchange price and willingness-to-pay signals, so only critical loads pay peak prices.
Concerns centre on smart meters and their remote control and variable pricing, on cyberattack vulnerability, and on the need for a business case before a utility invests.
